title: Oil, gas and offshore, 16 days of posts

clusters.text: The Houthis threatened to strike Saudi Aramco's headquarters and Riyadh refinery if Saudi Arabia hits Sanaa's oil depot.
clusters.verdict_basis: Reuters reporting, carried by SCMP and US News, says the Houthis threatened a "harsh and painful" response to Saudi-led strikes on Sanaa. It says spokesman Yahya Saree named the Saudi Aramco headquarters in Dhahran and an oil refinery in Riyadh as possible targets. The threat followed the coalition's evacuation order for the Yemen Petroleum Company's Sabah (al-Sabah) fuel depot on Sanaa's outskirts, which the coalition then struck. Al Jazeera likewise describes the threat as a reaction to that order. The claim's wording is accurate, though it is now incomplete. Al Jazeera, France 24 and the Korea Times report that the Houthis then claimed attacks on Aramco in Dhahran and on a Riyadh refinery, and Saudi officials confirmed a strike on an Aramco building in Dhahran. The claim has no obvious connection to Texas politics. I judged only its accuracy.

lanes.label: Texas oil as security and affordability

clusters.text: Saudi Arabia struck Sanaa's Al-Sabaha oil depot, triggering Houthi retaliation threats.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The strike is well documented. 
The Saudi-led coalition confirmed on Tuesday (Oct 13) that it had targeted a Yemeni oil company facility in Sanaa.
 
Coalition spokesman Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki said the Houthis used the Yemen Petroleum Company's al-Sabaha facility to fuel their war effort.
 The BBC (via Yahoo), Al Jazeera, the Times of Israel and France 24 all report it. The Houthi threats are also documented. 
Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree warned that any strike on Sanaa would meet a "harsh and painful" reprisal on Riyadh.
 
The Houthis then reportedly targeted an Aramco administrative building in Dhahran, according to Saudi SPA.
 
Saree also said operations toward Saudi depths would continue, targeting airports and oil facilities.


Two nuances. The strike came from the Saudi-led coalition, which is the usual shorthand for Saudi Arabia. The first Houthi threats were made in response to the coalition's evacuation warning, before the strike itself, so "triggering" is loosely worded. The Houthis did follow up with more threats and an actual attack after the strike. None of this changes the claim's substance. The Texas oil-policy context has no bearing on it.

lanes.label: Texas oil as security and affordability

clusters.text: The IEA says global diesel shortages will last well into 2027.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The IEA's October 2026 Oil Market Report (published Oct 14) has a section headed "Gasoil and diesel market tightness set to extend into 2027." 
The section covers diesel market tightness extending into 2027.
 Reuters, via BOE Report, reported that 
constrained diesel supplies could persist well into next year
. CNBC reported that the IEA 
said supply would remain tight into the latter half of 2027
, and that 
replenishing lost inventories may not begin before the second half of 2027
. The claim's wording ("global diesel shortages will last well into 2027") is slightly firmer than the IEA's hedged language ("could persist," "likely to persist"). It also describes a global market tightness, not a Texas matter. The core attribution, the timing and the "well into 2027" phrasing all match the IEA and the news coverage, so the gist is accurate.

lanes.label: Texas oil as security and affordability

clusters.text: Democrats have no proposal or plan to lower prices, especially gas.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The records contradict the claim as worded. The Texas Tribune's Oct. 8, 2026 candidate guide (via Yahoo) says Democratic governor nominee Gina Hinojosa 
has called for a pause on the state and federal gas taxes
. It says Senate nominee James Talarico 
has called for a pause on federal gas and diesel taxes and an end to the war with Iran
. The Dallas Morning News and WFAA report the same Hinojosa and Talarico gas-tax proposals. At the federal level, Sens. Mark Kelly and Richard Blumenthal introduced the Gas Prices Relief Act, which 
would temporarily suspend the 18.4 cents-per-gallon federal gas tax through October 1, 2026
. Rep. Dina Titus introduced a bill on Oct. 15 on fuel-efficiency standards, with the stated aim of countering high gas prices. Experts quoted by the Tribune 
widely pan proposals to suspend the state and federal gas tax
, and Republicans such as Gov. Abbott's office and Sen. Cornyn have opposed them. Critics can fairly dispute whether the proposals would work, but "no proposal or plan" is inaccurate because Democrats have made specific, documented proposals.

lanes.label: Texas oil as security and affordability

clusters.text: Democrats created the cost of living crisis.
clusters.verdict_basis: The claim is a sweeping causal and partisan statement, and the records don't support it as worded. The Congressional Research Service says the 2021–22 inflation began with COVID-19 supply disruptions, was worsened by the war in Ukraine, and was also fed by "unprecedented fiscal and monetary stimulus" (https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47273). Stimulus was passed under presidents of both parties. Economists disagree about how much each factor mattered: Richmond Fed and New York Fed work stresses supply-side factors, while an MIT Sloan summary of new research emphasizes federal spending (https://www.richmondfed.org/publications/research/econ_focus/2022/q3_feature2, https://mitsloan.mit.edu/ideas-made-to-matter/federal-spending-was-responsible-2022-spike-inflation-research-shows). Some Democratic-backed spending is a defensible contributor, but no source says one party "created" the crisis. For Texas specifically, the Dallas Fed attributes rising home-insurance costs to construction costs, climate risk and reinsurance costs, not to one party (https://www.dallasfed.org/research/swe/2026/swe2609).
